title: CSS Architecture at Scale
summary: Global CSS survives a handful of pages before collisions start. Learn how BEM, CSS Modules, CSS-in-JS, and utility-first each solve the scoping problem differently, and the real trade-offs between them.

slides.markdown:
CSS has exactly one global namespace. Every selector in every stylesheet loaded on a page competes with every other selector, forever, with no built-in module boundary. That works fine for a five-page marketing site and becomes a genuine engineering problem once dozens of teams are shipping components into the same app.

The symptom is always the same: someone adds `.card` in their feature, and it silently collides with a `.card` written by a different team eighteen months ago in a completely unrelated part of the codebase — because the cascade, covered in the [previous topic](css-cascade-and-specificity), doesn't know or care about team boundaries.

Every approach in this topic — BEM, CSS Modules, CSS-in-JS, utility-first — is solving the same underlying problem: **giving CSS a scoping mechanism the language never had.** They just do it at different points in the build/runtime pipeline, with different trade-offs.

slides.subTitle: Naming convention as scoping discipline
slides.markdown:
BEM (Block, Element, Modifier) is pure convention — no tooling required, just a naming discipline that makes collisions structurally unlikely:

```css
.card { }              /* Block */
.card__title { }       /* Element — a part of the block */
.card--featured { }    /* Modifier — a variant of the block */
.card__title--large { } /* Element with its own modifier */
```

Because every class is prefixed with its block name, `.card__title` from the checkout feature and a hypothetical `.dashboard__title` never collide — the prefix itself acts as the scope. The trade-off is that BEM enforces nothing at build time: a developer can still write plain `.card` instead of `.checkout-card`, and nothing stops them. It's discipline, not isolation, which is exactly why teams eventually reach for build-time or runtime tooling as the codebase grows past what code review can catch.

slides.subTitle: Build-time scoping via generated class names
Styling tied directly to components
Trading semantic classes for composition speed
slides.markdown:
Utility-first CSS (Tailwind is the dominant example) takes the opposite approach to all three above: instead of naming a semantic class and defining its properties, you compose pre-defined, single-purpose utility classes directly in markup: ```html
...
``` There's no `.card` class to collide with anything, because there's no custom class at all — every class (`p-4`, `rounded-lg`) is a shared, framework-defined atom with a fixed, single-purpose definition and near-identical specificity, so there's structurally nothing to fight over. The scoping problem is sidestepped entirely rather than solved. The trade-off is legibility and markup verbosity: a component with a dozen utility classes reads less like semantic HTML and more like inline styles with extra steps, and a design change that used to mean editing one CSS rule now means find-and-replacing a utility string across every usage — mitigated in practice by extracting repeated utility combinations into a component abstraction (a React component, a Vue single-file component) rather than a CSS class.

slides.sectionTitle: BEM vs CSS Modules vs CSS-in-JS vs utility-first
slides.markdown:
| | Scoping mechanism | Bundle/runtime cost | Best fit |
|---|---|---|
| **BEM** | naming convention only | none — plain CSS | small teams, no build-tool buy-in needed |
| **CSS Modules** | build-time class renaming | build step only, no runtime cost | component libraries wanting real isolation with plain CSS syntax |
| **CSS-in-JS** | build or runtime class generation | runtime cost for classic variants; near-zero for compile-time variants | heavy dynamic/prop-driven styling |
| **Utility-first** | shared low-specificity atoms | near-zero runtime; larger initial CSS payload, aggressively purged in practice | design systems prioritizing consistency and composition speed over semantic markup |

The honest takeaway: there is no universally "best" option here — the right choice depends on whether the team values semantic class names, whether dynamic styling is common, and how much runtime cost is tolerable. Real large codebases sometimes mix two of these (utility classes for spacing/layout, CSS Modules for a handful of genuinely complex components) rather than picking one dogmatically.

The four approaches split cleanly along *when* the scoping decision is made: BEM resolves nothing automatically — the developer resolves it by hand, at write time, through discipline. CSS Modules resolve scoping at **build time** — the bundler rewrites class names before any code ships. Classic CSS-in-JS resolves it at **runtime** — the browser executes JS that generates and injects styles as the component renders. Utility-first resolves it at **build time** too, but by pre-generating a fixed set of atoms rather than rewriting per-component names — and by *purging* unused utility classes from the final CSS bundle so the payload only includes what's actually used.

slides.subTitle: "How would you structure CSS for a 200-component design system"
slides.markdown:
This live-design-conversation prompt is really asking whether you can reason about trade-offs at scale rather than name-drop a framework. A strong answer surfaces the actual axes that matter at 200 components across multiple consuming teams:

- **Isolation guarantee** — at this scale, convention-only scoping (BEM) is too fragile; you want a build-time or structural guarantee.
- **Consistency enforcement** — a design system's whole point is visual consistency, which argues for a constrained set of tokens/utilities over freeform per-component CSS.
- **Consumer flexibility** — will consuming teams need to override styles for edge cases? Heavy CSS-in-JS with deeply specific generated selectors can make overrides painful; utility classes are trivially overridable by adding another utility.
- **Team's existing tooling** — CSS Modules assume a bundler; utility-first assumes buy-in on writing markup differently.

A design system built on CSS Modules or utility-first, both wrapped in `@layer` so consumer overrides have a predictable, guaranteed place to slot in, is a common real answer — but naming the axes above matters more than landing on a specific stack.

The pitfall in a real migration (say, global CSS to CSS Modules) is treating it as a big-bang rewrite instead of an incremental one — freezing feature work for weeks to convert every stylesheet at once is rarely something a business will actually accept, and a half-finished big-bang migration is worse than the problem it was solving.

The approach that works in practice: new components adopt the new system immediately; old components stay on the old system until they're touched for an unrelated reason, at which point they're converted as part of that change. This means both systems coexist for a while — which is fine, since CSS Modules and global CSS can load on the same page without conflicting, precisely because CSS Modules' whole purpose is not colliding with anything else.

The actual risk to watch for during coexistence: a converted component's old global class name might still be referenced by some other unconverted file's selector (`.old-card .icon { }` reaching into a component that no longer has `.old-card` in its markup) — a grep for cross-file references before deleting an old class name catches this before it ships silently broken.

slides.sectionTitle: Specificity still matters inside every approach
slides.markdown:
None of these four approaches eliminate the [cascade](css-cascade-and-specificity) — they change what collides, not how collisions resolve once they happen. CSS Modules and utility-first both work partly *because* they keep generated/utility selectors at a uniformly low, single-class specificity, so on the rare occasion two of them do compete, source order (not an unpredictable tuple mismatch) decides it — a deliberate, not incidental, property of both systems.

CSS-in-JS libraries occasionally generate deeply nested selectors for pseudo-states or theming, which can reintroduce real specificity fights if not watched — a component library with `.sc-bdVaJa:hover .sc-htpNat` style generated selectors can be surprisingly hard for a consumer to override, which is one of the less-discussed downsides of the approach.

The takeaway: architecture choices manage the *scale* of the cascade problem, but understanding the cascade itself, from the previous topic, is still what you reach for the moment two scoped styles genuinely need to compete.

slides.sectionTitle: Naming the trade-off, not the winner
slides.markdown:
There's no interview-safe "correct" answer to "which CSS architecture is best" — every real engineering org has shipped successful products on more than one of these. What signals seniority is naming the actual trade-off you're making and why it fits the situation in front of you: "I'd reach for CSS Modules here because the team already has a bundler and wants real isolation without changing how they write CSS day to day" is a stronger answer than "CSS Modules are the best practice."

The weakest answer in this space is picking a favorite from a past job and defending it as universally correct — every one of these four approaches has a real, documented cost, and pretending otherwise is usually the tell that the candidate hasn't shipped with more than one of them.
